# How to use this guide

Hospital and Clinical Pharmacy is a 75-hour second-year D.Pharm theory subject (3 hours a week) with a 25-hour practical (ER20-25P). The syllabus lists 12 chapters (the PCI table numbers them 1, 2 and 4 to 13; the committees chapter carries the infection control committee as well). In this guide the large chapters are split and the very short ones are joined, so there are 12 units:

| Guide unit | Syllabus chapter | Hours in syllabus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Hospital pharmacy – organisation, standards, NQAS, NABH | 1 | 6 |
| 2. Committees (P&T, Infection Control) and hospital formulary | 2 | 4 |
| 3. Drug lists, purchase procedures and inventory control | 4 (first half) | 14 shared |
| 4. Central drug store, cold chain, expiry, disposal, documentation | 4 (second half) | 14 shared |
| 5. Drug distribution | 5 | 7 |
| 6. Compounding, IV admixtures and TPN | 6 | 4 |
| 7. Radiopharmaceuticals and computers in hospital pharmacy | 7 and 8 | 2 + 2 |
| 8. Clinical pharmacy – development, clinical terms, daily activities | 9 (first part) | 12 shared |
| 9. Pharmaceutical care, drug-related problems, MTM, HMR | 9 (second part) | 12 shared |
| 10. Clinical laboratory tests | 10 | 10 |
| 11. Poisoning and drug/poison information centres | 11 | 6 |
| 12. Pharmacovigilance, medication errors and drug interactions | 12 and 13 | 2 + 6 |

Study one unit every two or three days. Read the notes, redo every worked example with your own numbers, draw the flow charts once from memory, and then answer the question bank without looking. Units 3, 4, 8, 9 and 10 carry the most hours – give them extra time.

## Exam pattern (ER-2020 theory paper)

D.Pharm ER-2020 examinations are yearly. The theory paper is **80 marks, 3 hours**; another 20 marks come from sessional (internal) assessment. The usual ER-2020 board paper looks like this. Confirm the exact split with your college, because boards sometimes change the format.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | Objective questions (MCQs / one-word / fill in the blanks) – all compulsory | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| II | Short answers – attempt 10 of 11 | 10 × 3 = 30 |
| III | Long answers – attempt 6 of 7 | 6 × 5 = 30 |

In this guide the **long** questions are 5-mark answers and the **short** questions are 3-mark answers, to match this pattern. A few **very-short** (2-mark) questions are included for quick revision and for sessional tests.

The practical examination (ER20-25P) is assessed separately; the practical guides in this pack follow the eight experiments in the syllabus.

## Probability ratings

- **High** – asked in most years; prepare the full answer with flow charts, tables and examples.
- **Medium** – asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** – rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

Ratings are an estimate from the syllabus weight and the kind of questions usually set in D.Pharm papers. They are not a promise.

## Scoring tips for Hospital and Clinical Pharmacy

1. **Begin every answer with a definition.** Hospital formulary, pharmaceutical care, unit dose, pharmacovigilance, medication error, drug interaction – examiners look for it first.
2. **Use flow charts** for processes: tender procedure, unit-dose distribution, IV admixture preparation, pharmaceutical care cycle, drug information query, management of poisoning.
3. **Use tables for comparisons:** FIFO vs FEFO, floor stock vs unit dose, ABC vs VED, primary vs secondary vs tertiary sources, Type A vs Type B ADRs, obstructive vs restrictive PFT, MTM vs HMR.
4. **Show calculations step by step** – EOQ, reorder level, inventory turnover, ABC cut-offs, drops per minute, creatinine clearance, child dose, radioactive decay, TPN calories. Write the formula, put in the numbers with units, and box the answer.
5. **Quote standard numbers correctly:** cold chain 2–8 °C; Schedule H1 register kept 3 years; Naranjo ≥9 definite, 5–8 probable; Na 135–145 and K 3.5–5.0 mmol/L; INR 2–3 for warfarin; FEV1/FVC below 0.70 = obstruction; Tc-99m half-life about 6 hours.
6. **Name examples:** high-alert drugs, reserve antibiotics, LASA pairs in Tall Man letters, antidotes with their poisons, enzyme inducers and inhibitors.
7. **For a 5-mark long answer**, aim for about one and a half pages: definition, classification or table, flow chart, 4–6 explained points, advantages and disadvantages, and the pharmacist's role.
8. **For a 3-mark short answer**, write 5–6 crisp points or a small table; do not write an essay.
9. **Always add "role of the pharmacist"** where it fits (committees, AMR, NABH, PV, medication errors) – it is the heart of this subject.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you have only a few hours, learn these with full flow charts and tables: **P&T Committee and hospital formulary**, **tender procedure**, **EOQ, reorder level and ABC/VED** (with a calculation), **cold chain**, **unit-dose system vs floor stock**, **IV admixtures and incompatibilities**, **TPN**, **pharmaceutical care and DRPs**, **daily activities of the clinical pharmacist**, **LFT/RFT/electrolytes**, **antidotes**, **drug information sources**, **pharmacovigilance and PvPI**, **medication errors and LASA**, **drug interactions**.

## Hospital pharmacy and committees (Units 1–2)

| Item | Key point |

# Systematic approach to drug information queries

**Aim:** To answer two drug information queries in a systematic way using primary, secondary and tertiary sources of information, and to document the response.

> The cases below are worked examples. Your teacher will give you your own queries; follow the same steps and record them in the query form.

## Principle

A good answer depends on understanding the **real question** behind the request and on using reliable, current sources in a logical order. The **modified systematic approach** has seven steps:

```text
1. Secure demographics of the requester (name, profession, contact, urgency)
2. Obtain background information (patient age, weight, diagnosis,
   other drugs, kidney/liver function, why the question is asked)
3. Determine and categorise the ultimate question
   (dose, ADR, interaction, pregnancy/lactation, compatibility, poisoning…)
4. Develop a search strategy and search:
   tertiary → secondary → primary
5. Evaluate, analyse and put together the information
6. Formulate and give the response (verbal and written, with references)
7. Follow up and document
```

## Requirements

Drug information request/response form, standard references (National Formulary of India, CIMS/IDR, Martindale, BNF, Goodman & Gilman, a pregnancy and lactation reference, an interaction reference), computer with internet access to PubMed and other databases, telephone, register or database for documentation.

## Procedure

1. Receive the query in person or by telephone; write the requester's details and the time.
2. Ask open questions to collect background details; restate the question to confirm it.
3. Classify the query and note how urgent it is.
4. Search a tertiary source first for a quick, reliable answer; if more recent or detailed information is needed, search PubMed (secondary) for primary articles.
5. Compare sources; note agreements and differences; judge quality.
6. Write a clear answer: direct answer first, then the reasons, with references.
7. Communicate the answer within the time needed; record it on the form.
8. Follow up with the requester (was the advice used, what was the outcome?).

## Observations (worked cases)

**Case 1 – pregnancy query.** A doctor in the antenatal clinic asks: "Can a pregnant woman at 10 weeks take ondansetron for vomiting?"

| Step | Record |
| --- | --- |
| Requester | Resident doctor, obstetrics OPD; answer needed in 30 minutes |
| Background | 26-year-old, 10 weeks pregnant, persistent vomiting, no other drugs, normal kidney function |
| Category | Drug use in pregnancy (first trimester) |
| Tertiary search | National Formulary of India; pregnancy and lactation reference |
| Secondary/primary | PubMed: recent studies on ondansetron in early pregnancy |
| Evaluation | First-line advice is lifestyle measures and drugs with long safety experience; ondansetron is used when others fail; some studies suggest a small possible risk of certain birth defects in the first trimester while others do not |
| Response | Try first-line options as per the obstetric protocol; if vomiting continues, the obstetrician may use ondansetron after discussing the small uncertain risk; ensure fluids and electrolytes |
| Follow-up | Called next day – first-line drug given, vomiting controlled |

**Case 2 – IV compatibility query.** A staff nurse in the ICU asks whether phenytoin can be infused in 5% dextrose.

| Step | Record |
| --- | --- |
| Requester | ICU staff nurse, urgent |
| Background | Adult with seizures, phenytoin loading dose ordered; only dextrose line running |
| Category | IV compatibility |
| Tertiary search | Injectable drug compatibility reference |
| Evaluation | Phenytoin precipitates in dextrose solutions |
| Response | Do not mix with dextrose; dilute in 0.9% sodium chloride, give through a separate line or flush the line with saline before and after, use an in-line filter if required, and give at the recommended slow rate with monitoring |
| Follow-up | Infusion given in saline without problems |

## Result

Two drug information queries were answered systematically using tertiary, secondary and primary sources, and the responses were documented.

## Precautions

1. Always find the real question and the patient details before searching.
2. Use current editions and reliable sources; note the edition and date.
3. Do not give an answer you are unsure of – say when you will call back.
4. Keep patient information confidential.
5. Record every query, even simple ones.

## Viva questions

1. **What are tertiary sources? Give examples.** Compiled summaries – textbooks, compendia, databases (Martindale, BNF, NFI, CIMS).
2. **Why start with tertiary sources?** They are quick, easy and reliable for most questions.
3. **Give one advantage and one disadvantage of primary literature.** Most current and detailed; needs skill to evaluate and is voluminous.
4. **What is the "ultimate question"?** The real need behind the request, found from background information.
5. **Why is follow-up needed?** To know whether the advice helped and to improve the service.
practicals.title: Systematic approach to drug information queries

# Interpretation of laboratory reports to optimise drug therapy

**Aim:** To interpret the laboratory reports of two clinical cases and suggest how the drug therapy should be adjusted.

> The cases below are worked examples. Use the reference range printed on the report you are given; values here are typical adult ranges.

## Principle

Laboratory values show how well the kidney, liver, blood, thyroid and heart are working. Many drugs must be **chosen, dosed or monitored** according to these values – for example renally cleared drugs by creatinine clearance, warfarin by INR and potassium-affecting drugs by serum potassium. The pharmacist compares each value with the reference range, links abnormal values to the disease or a drug, and makes a recommendation.

## Requirements

Case sheets with laboratory reports, reference range chart, a renal dosing reference, calculator, case work-up form.

## Procedure

1. Read the patient details: age, sex, weight, diagnosis and drug chart.
2. List every laboratory value with its reference range; mark high (H) and low (L).
3. Calculate derived values: creatinine clearance (Cockcroft–Gault), anion gap, corrected values where needed.
4. Decide what each abnormal value means: disease, drug effect, or both.
5. Check each drug for dose adjustment, contraindication or monitoring need.
6. Write recommendations and a monitoring plan in SOAP format.

## Observations and calculations

**Case 1.** Man, 65 years, 60 kg, admitted with pneumonia and heart failure. Drugs: gentamicin 80 mg IV every 8 h, furosemide 40 mg twice daily, digoxin 0.25 mg once daily, enalapril 5 mg twice daily.

| Test | Result | Reference | Remark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Serum creatinine | 1.8 mg/dL | 0.6–1.2 | H |
| Blood urea | 68 mg/dL | 15–40 | H |
| Potassium | 3.0 mmol/L | 3.5–5.0 | L |
| Sodium | 136 mmol/L | 135–145 | Normal |

```text
CrCl = [(140 − 65) × 60] / (72 × 1.8) = (75 × 60) / 129.6 = 4500 / 129.6 ≈ 35 mL/min
```

Interpretation and recommendations:

1. Reduced kidney function (CrCl about 35 mL/min) → gentamicin and digoxin accumulate. Suggest a longer gentamicin dosing interval or another antibiotic, with serum gentamicin levels; review digoxin dose and check a digoxin level.
2. Low potassium (likely from furosemide) increases the risk of **digoxin toxicity** → potassium replacement and monitoring.
3. Monitor creatinine, potassium and urine output daily; watch for nausea, visual changes or irregular pulse (digoxin toxicity).

**Case 2.** Woman, 52 years, on warfarin for atrial fibrillation, recently started on a course of metronidazole for a dental infection. Complains of gum bleeding.

| Test | Result | Reference / target | Remark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| INR | 5.2 | target 2–3 | H |
| Haemoglobin | 10.8 g/dL | 12–15 | L |
| Platelets | 2.4 lakh/µL | 1.5–4.5 lakh | Normal |

Interpretation and recommendations:

1. INR far above target with bleeding → **drug interaction**: metronidazole inhibits warfarin metabolism.
2. Recommend: withhold warfarin as per protocol, give vitamin K as decided by the physician, choose an alternative antibiotic if possible, recheck INR daily until back in range, then restart warfarin at an adjusted dose.
3. Low haemoglobin – monitor for continued blood loss.
4. Counsel the patient to report bleeding and to tell every doctor that she takes warfarin.

## Result

Laboratory reports of two cases were interpreted, abnormal values were linked to the disease and drugs, and dose and monitoring recommendations were made.

## Precautions

1. Always use the laboratory's own reference range and units.
2. Look at trends, not a single value.
3. Use actual body weight carefully in obese or oedematous patients.
4. Recommendations go to the prescriber; the pharmacist does not change orders alone.

## Viva questions

1. **Write the Cockcroft–Gault equation.** CrCl = (140 − age) × weight / (72 × SCr), × 0.85 for women.
2. **Why is low potassium dangerous with digoxin?** It increases digoxin binding and toxicity (arrhythmias).
3. **What is the usual INR target for warfarin?** 2–3 for most indications.
4. **Name two drugs that raise serum potassium.** ACE inhibitors and spironolactone.
5. **What does a high ALT suggest?** Liver-cell damage (hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury).
practicals.title: Interpretation of laboratory reports to optimise drug therapy

# Filling the IPC ADR reporting form and causality assessment

**Aim:** To fill the Suspected Adverse Drug Reaction Reporting Form of the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (PvPI) for two cases and to assess causality using the WHO-UMC scale and the Naranjo algorithm.

> Use the current version of the form available from IPC or your ADR monitoring centre. The cases below are worked examples.

## Principle

Spontaneous reporting of suspected ADRs is the backbone of pharmacovigilance. Under the **Pharmacovigilance Programme of India (PvPI)**, health professionals report on the IPC form to an ADR monitoring centre, which sends it to the National Coordination Centre at IPC, Ghaziabad. **Causality assessment** judges how likely it is that the drug caused the event. Certainty is **not** needed before reporting.

## Requirements

Blank IPC Suspected ADR Reporting Forms, case details, WHO-UMC causality table, Naranjo questionnaire, pen.

## Procedure

1. Read the case carefully; list all drugs with dates.
2. Fill the form section by section:
   - **Patient information** – initials (not the full name), age or date of birth, sex, weight.
   - **Suspected adverse reaction** – date of onset and recovery, description of the reaction, relevant tests, seriousness (death, life-threatening, hospitalisation, disability, congenital anomaly, other medically important), outcome (recovered, recovering, not recovered, fatal, unknown).
   - **Suspected medication(s)** – brand and generic name, manufacturer, batch number, expiry date, dose, route, frequency, start and stop dates, reason for use; action taken (withdrawn, dose reduced, no change); whether the reaction reduced after stopping (dechallenge) and reappeared on restarting (rechallenge); concomitant drugs and relevant history.
   - **Reporter details** – name, profession, address, contact, signature and date.
3. Assess causality using the WHO-UMC scale and the Naranjo algorithm.
4. Submit the form to the ADR monitoring centre (or online); keep a copy.

## Observations and calculations

**Case 1.** A 34-year-old man (62 kg) started co-trimoxazole for a urinary infection. On day 2 he developed an itchy red rash over the trunk. No other new drugs. Co-trimoxazole was stopped and the rash disappeared in 4 days. Not restarted.

| Naranjo question | Answer | Score |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Previous conclusive reports on this reaction? | Yes | +1 |
| 2. Event appeared after the suspected drug was given? | Yes | +2 |
| 3. Improved when drug stopped or antagonist given? | Yes | +1 |
| 4. Reappeared when drug given again? | Not done | 0 |
| 5. Alternative causes that could cause the reaction? | No | +2 |
| 6. Reappeared with placebo? | Not done | 0 |
| 7. Drug detected in blood in toxic concentration? | Not done | 0 |
| 8. Dose-related severity? | Not known | 0 |
| 9. Similar reaction to the same or similar drug before? | Not known | 0 |
| 10. Confirmed by objective evidence? | Yes (seen by doctor) | +1 |
| **Total** | | **7 – probable** |

WHO-UMC: reasonable time relationship, unlikely to be due to disease or other drugs, improved on withdrawal, no rechallenge → **probable/likely**. Seriousness: non-serious. Outcome: recovered.

**Case 2.** A 58-year-old woman on enalapril 5 mg twice daily for 6 weeks developed a dry, irritating cough. She is a non-smoker with no chest infection; chest X-ray normal. Enalapril was replaced by losartan; the cough settled in 3 weeks. Earlier, she had stopped enalapril for a week and the cough had eased, returning when she restarted it.

| Naranjo question | Answer | Score |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Previous conclusive reports? | Yes | +1 |
| 2. After the drug was given? | Yes | +2 |
| 3. Improved on stopping? | Yes | +1 |
| 4. Reappeared on re-administration? | Yes | +2 |
| 5. Alternative causes? | No | +2 |
| 6. Placebo? | Not done | 0 |
| 7. Toxic blood levels? | Not done | 0 |
| 8. Dose-related? | Not known | 0 |
| 9. Previous similar reaction? | Not known | 0 |
| 10. Objective evidence? | Yes (clinical exam, normal X-ray) | +1 |
| **Total** | | **9 – definite** |

WHO-UMC: positive dechallenge and rechallenge, no other cause → **certain**. Type A ADR (related to the drug's action on bradykinin).

**Naranjo interpretation:** ≥9 definite; 5–8 probable; 1–4 possible; ≤0 doubtful.

## Result

Two suspected ADRs were reported on the IPC form; causality was assessed as probable (co-trimoxazole rash) and definite/certain (enalapril cough).

## Precautions

1. Use only patient initials to protect privacy.
2. Fill batch number and dates accurately.
3. Report even when unsure – causality is assessed later.
4. Report serious reactions as early as possible.
5. Do not deliberately rechallenge a patient just to confirm a reaction.

## Viva questions

1. **Where is the National Coordination Centre of PvPI?** Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad.
2. **What is dechallenge?** Stopping the suspected drug and observing whether the reaction improves.
3. **Name two causality scales.** WHO-UMC and Naranjo.
4. **What makes an ADR "serious"?** Death, life-threatening, hospitalisation, disability, congenital anomaly or other medically important event.
5. **Can a patient report an ADR?** Yes – a consumer form and helpline (1800-180-3024) are available.
practicals.title: Filling the IPC ADR reporting form and causality assessment

# Orthopaedic and surgical aids

**Aim:** To identify common orthopaedic and surgical aids – knee cap, lumbo-sacral (LS) belt, abdominal belt, walker and walking stick – and to demonstrate their selection, fitting and use.

## Principle

Orthopaedic aids **support, immobilise or relieve load** on joints, muscles and the spine, and mobility aids help patients walk safely by widening the base of support. Pharmacists in hospitals and community pharmacies supply these aids, so they must know the indications, how to choose the correct size, how to fit them and how to teach the patient.

## Requirements

Knee caps (elastic knee supports) of different sizes, LS belt, abdominal belt (binder), adjustable walker, walking stick (single-point and tripod/quadripod), measuring tape, size charts of the manufacturer, a chair.

## Procedure

### Knee cap (knee support)

1. Uses: mild knee pain, osteoarthritis, minor sprains, support during activity; gives compression and warmth.
2. Measure the circumference around the middle of the knee cap (or as the size chart directs) with the leg straight; choose the size from the chart.
3. Slip it on from the foot upward; centre the opening (if any) over the patella; smooth out wrinkles.
4. It should be snug but not tight – check that there is no numbness, tingling, swelling below or colour change of the foot.
5. Remove at night unless advised; wash as directed.

### Lumbo-sacral (LS) belt

1. Uses: low back pain, lumbar disc problems, support after spinal injury or surgery, heavy lifting.
2. Measure the waist (or hip) circumference as the size chart directs.
3. Apply in standing or lying position; the rigid back stays (supports) lie over the lower spine; fasten the front Velcro starting at the bottom, firm but allowing normal breathing.
4. Advise: wear during activity, not continuously for long periods (muscles may weaken); combine with exercises advised by the physiotherapist.

### Abdominal belt (abdominal binder)

1. Uses: support after abdominal surgery or caesarean section, after delivery, hernia support (as advised), to reduce pain on coughing and movement.
2. Measure the circumference at the widest part of the abdomen; select the size.
3. Apply lying down; centre on the abdomen, overlap and fasten from below upward; it should be firm without restricting breathing.
4. Check the skin daily for redness; keep the wound dressing clean underneath.

### Walker

1. Uses: elderly patients, weakness after illness or surgery, poor balance, partial weight-bearing after leg injury.
2. Adjust height: with the patient standing upright and arms hanging, the walker handles should be at the level of the wrist crease; the elbows bend slightly (about 15–30°) when holding it.
3. Walking: move the walker forward about one step's length → step forward with the weak leg → then the strong leg; keep all four legs on the ground before stepping.
4. Sitting: back up until the chair touches the legs, reach back for the armrests, lower slowly – do not lean on the walker while sitting down.

### Walking stick (cane)

1. Uses: mild balance problems, mild weakness or pain in one leg.
2. Height: handle at the level of the wrist crease with the arm hanging; elbow slightly bent when holding.
3. Hold the stick in the hand **opposite** the weak or painful leg.
4. Move the stick and the weak leg forward together, then the strong leg.
5. On stairs: "up with the good, down with the bad" – the strong leg leads going up; the stick and weak leg lead going down.
6. Check the rubber tip regularly; tripod/quadripod sticks give more support.

## Observations

| Aid | Patient measurement | Size selected | Fit check |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Knee cap | Knee circumference ___ cm | ___ | Snug, no numbness or swelling |
| LS belt | Waist ___ cm | ___ | Stays over lower spine, breathing normal |
| Abdominal belt | Abdomen ___ cm | ___ | Firm, skin not pinched |
| Walker | Wrist crease height ___ cm | Set to ___ | Elbow bend about 15–30° |
| Walking stick | Wrist crease height ___ cm | Set to ___ | Held in hand opposite weak leg |

## Result

The orthopaedic and surgical aids were identified, the correct size was selected, and their fitting and use were demonstrated.

## Precautions

1. Always measure; do not guess the size.
2. Too tight supports reduce circulation; too loose ones give no support.
3. Check rubber tips and locks on walkers and sticks.
4. Do not use support belts as a substitute for exercise and medical advice.
5. Remove supports and seek advice if pain, swelling, numbness or skin damage occurs.

## Viva questions

1. **In which hand is a walking stick held?** In the hand opposite the weak or painful leg.
2. **How is walker height adjusted?** Handles at the wrist crease with arms hanging; elbows slightly bent when holding.
3. **What is an LS belt used for?** Support of the lower back in low back pain and after spinal injury or surgery.
4. **Why should support belts not be worn all the time?** Long continuous use can weaken the supporting muscles.
5. **What is the rule for stairs with a stick?** Up with the good leg, down with the bad leg.
practicals.title: Orthopaedic and surgical aids (knee cap, LS belt, abdominal belt, walker, walking sticks)

# Types of bandages and dressing materials

**Aim:** To identify common surgical dressing materials and bandages – sterile gauze, absorbent cotton, roller, crepe, triangular and tubular bandages – and to demonstrate the basic bandaging turns.

## Principle

**Dressings** are applied directly on a wound to protect it, absorb discharge and help healing. **Bandages** hold dressings or splints in place, give support or compression, and limit movement. Surgical dressing materials such as absorbent gauze and absorbent cotton wool have pharmacopoeial standards. A bandage must be firm enough to do its job without cutting off circulation.

## Requirements

Sterile gauze swabs and pads, absorbent cotton wool, roller bandages (cotton), crepe (elastic) bandages of different widths, triangular bandage, tubular bandage, adhesive tape, safety pins or clips, scissors, mannequin or volunteer.

## Identification of materials

| Material | Description | Main uses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Sterile absorbent gauze** | Cotton cloth of open weave, sterilised and packed as swabs or pads | Primary dressing on wounds, cleaning wounds, packing |
| **Absorbent cotton wool** | Cleaned, bleached cotton fibres that absorb fluid | Padding, cleaning skin before injections (with antiseptic), absorbent layer over gauze (never directly on an open wound – fibres stick) |
| **Roller bandage (cotton)** | Long strip rolled up | Holding dressings in place |
| **Crepe bandage** | Elastic cotton bandage that stretches and recovers | Support and compression of sprains and strains, holding dressings on joints, controlling swelling |
| **Triangular bandage** | Large triangle of cloth | Arm sling, head bandage, holding large dressings, first aid |
| **Tubular bandage** | Seamless elastic tube | Quick support for limbs and fingers, holding dressings |
| **Adhesive tape** | Plaster tape | Fixing dressings and cannulae |

## Procedure – basic bandaging

1. Explain the procedure; make the patient comfortable with the part supported in the position it should stay in.
2. Wash hands; place a dressing over any wound first.
3. Hold the roll with the rolled part upward ("head" up) and unroll it close to the skin.
4. Start with **two circular turns** below the injury to anchor the bandage.
5. Bandage from **distal (far) to proximal (near the heart)**, covering one-half to two-thirds of the previous turn each time, with even tension.
6. Use the correct turn:
   - **Circular** – overlapping circles, for anchoring and for the wrist or forehead;
   - **Spiral** – for parts of even width (arm, finger);
   - **Reverse spiral** – for parts that widen (forearm, leg);
   - **Figure-of-eight** – for joints (ankle, elbow, knee);
   - **Spica** – figure-of-eight over a joint where a limb meets the trunk (shoulder, groin, thumb);
   - **Recurrent** – for the head or a stump.
7. Finish with a circular turn and fix with tape or clip (not over the wound or on the inner side of a limb).
8. **Check circulation** beyond the bandage: colour, warmth, capillary refill (pressed nail returns to pink within about 2 seconds), numbness or tingling.

**Arm sling with triangular bandage:** place the bandage with the point under the elbow, the forearm across the chest, bring the lower end up over the forearm and tie at the side of the neck; fold and pin the point at the elbow.

## Observations

| Bandage practised | Body part | Type of turn | Circulation check |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Crepe | Ankle | Figure-of-eight | Toes pink, warm |
| Roller | Forearm | Reverse spiral | Fingers pink, warm |
| Triangular | Forearm | Arm sling | Fingers pink, warm |

## Result

Dressing materials and bandages were identified, and common bandaging turns were demonstrated correctly with circulation checked afterwards.

## Precautions

1. Never apply a bandage too tight; recheck circulation after some time, especially with crepe bandages and swelling.
2. Do not put cotton wool directly on an open wound.
3. Use sterile gauze for wounds; keep the packet sealed until use.
4. Leave fingers and toes exposed to check circulation.
5. Do not tie knots over a wound or bony points.

## Viva questions

1. **Which turn is used for joints?** Figure-of-eight.
2. **Why bandage from distal to proximal?** To support venous return and avoid trapping fluid below the bandage.
3. **What is a crepe bandage used for?** Support and compression of sprains and strains and holding dressings on joints.
4. **Why is cotton wool not placed directly on wounds?** Fibres stick to the wound and are hard to remove.
5. **How do you check that a bandage is not too tight?** Colour, warmth, capillary refill and sensation of the part beyond it.
practicals.title: Types of bandages and dressing materials (gauze, cotton, crepe)

# Needles, syringes, catheters, IV sets and other medical devices

**Aim:** To identify and demonstrate the use of needles, syringes, IV cannulae, IV administration sets, urinary catheters and urine bags, Ryle's (nasogastric) tube, urine pots, colostomy bags and oxygen masks.

## Principle

Hospital pharmacies stock and issue many medical devices. The pharmacist must recognise each device, know its sizes and uses, store it correctly (sterile, dry, before expiry) and help nurses and patients use it safely. Most of these devices are **sterile and single-use**; reuse spreads infection.

## Requirements

Samples of hypodermic needles of different gauges, syringes (1 mL insulin, 2, 5, 10 mL, auto-disable syringe), IV cannulae of different sizes, IV infusion sets (macro-drip and micro-drip), Foley urinary catheter, urine collection bag, Ryle's tube, sterile urine container (urine pot), colostomy bags (one-piece and two-piece), nasal cannula, simple oxygen mask, venturi mask, non-rebreather mask, mannequin.

## Identification and use

| Device | Key features | Use and handling points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Hypodermic needle** | Size by **gauge** (larger number = thinner) and length | Thin needles (26–27 G) for intradermal/SC; 21–23 G for IM; never recap a used needle; discard in a puncture-proof sharps container |
| **Syringe** | Barrel, plunger, Luer slip or Luer lock tip; graduated in mL | Choose a size close to the volume; **insulin syringe** graduated in units (match syringe to insulin strength); **auto-disable syringe** locks after one use (immunisation) |
| **IV cannula** | Plastic catheter over a needle; size in gauge with standard colour coding (for example 18 G green, 20 G pink, 22 G blue, 24 G yellow) | Larger bore for blood and rapid fluids; smaller for children and routine drugs; fix with dressing and label date |
| **IV infusion set** | Spike, drip chamber, roller clamp, injection port, Luer connector | Macro-drip about 20 drops/mL (adults); micro-drip 60 drops/mL (children, precise drugs); prime to remove air; calculate drops per minute |
| **Foley urinary catheter** | Soft tube with an inflatable balloon; size in French (Fr) units; two-way or three-way | Urinary retention, monitoring output, surgery; inserted aseptically; balloon inflated with sterile water as stated on the catheter |
| **Urine collection bag** | Bag with tubing, non-return valve and drain tap; graduated | Keep below bladder level and off the floor; empty regularly; closed system to prevent infection |
| **Ryle's (nasogastric) tube** | Long tube with markings, passed through the nose into the stomach | Feeding, giving drugs, draining stomach contents; length estimated nose → ear → xiphisternum; position confirmed by aspirate testing or X-ray before use; flush before and after drugs |
| **Urine pot (container)** | Sterile screw-capped container | Mid-stream urine for culture and routine tests; label and send promptly |
| **Colostomy bag** | Pouch fixed over a stoma; one-piece or two-piece (flange + bag); drainable or closed | Measure stoma and cut the opening to fit, protect surrounding skin, empty or change as needed |
| **Nasal cannula** | Two prongs in the nostrils | Low-flow oxygen (about 1–4 L/min) |
| **Simple face mask** | Covers nose and mouth | Moderate oxygen (about 5–10 L/min) |
| **Venturi mask** | Colour-coded adaptors giving fixed oxygen concentrations | Patients needing controlled oxygen, e.g. COPD |
| **Non-rebreather mask** | Mask with reservoir bag and valves | High oxygen (about 10–15 L/min) in emergencies; reservoir kept inflated |

## Procedure

1. Identify each device and note its size markings, sterility and expiry date on the pack.
2. Demonstrate on the mannequin: drawing up a dose with a syringe; priming an IV set and counting drops; securing a cannula; connecting a urine bag to a catheter and positioning it; measuring and marking a Ryle's tube length; fitting a colostomy bag; selecting and fitting an oxygen device and setting the flow.
3. Show safe disposal: sharps in a puncture-proof white container; contaminated plastics (tubing, bags, catheters) in the red bag; soiled dressings in the yellow bag, as per the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules.

## Observations / calculations

**Drip rate check:** 500 mL normal saline over 4 h with a macro-drip set (20 drops/mL).

```text
Drops/min = (500 × 20) / (4 × 60) = 10,000 / 240 ≈ 42 drops/min
```

| Device | Size noted | Sterile/expiry checked | Demonstrated |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Needle | ___ G | Yes | Drawing up a dose |
| IV set | ___ drops/mL | Yes | Priming, drip rate |
| Ryle's tube | ___ Fr | Yes | Length measurement |

## Result

Common hospital medical devices were identified, their sizes and uses noted, and their correct use and disposal demonstrated.

## Precautions

1. Check sterility (intact pack) and expiry before use.
2. One needle, one syringe, one patient – never reuse.
3. Do not recap used needles; dispose immediately in sharps containers.
4. Keep urine bags below bladder level; never disconnect a closed system unnecessarily.
5. Confirm Ryle's tube position before every feed or drug.
6. Oxygen is a drug – give only at the prescribed flow; no smoking or flames nearby.

## Viva questions

1. **Which is thinner, a 22 G or an 18 G needle?** The 22 G needle (larger gauge number = thinner).
2. **What is an auto-disable syringe?** A syringe that locks after a single use; used in immunisation.
3. **How is the length of a Ryle's tube estimated?** Nose tip → ear lobe → xiphisternum.
4. **What are the drops per mL of a micro-drip set?** 60 drops/mL.
5. **Which oxygen device gives the highest concentration?** Non-rebreather mask with reservoir bag.

# Case studies on drug–drug interactions

**Aim:** To identify, interpret and report drug–drug interactions in two clinical cases and to recommend how to manage them.

> The cases below are worked examples. Your teacher will give you other cases; use an interaction reference to check each pair of drugs.

## Principle

A drug interaction occurs when one drug (the **precipitant**) changes the effect of another (the **object drug**). Interactions may be **pharmacokinetic** (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion) or **pharmacodynamic** (additive, synergistic or opposing effects). Their clinical significance depends on **severity** (major, moderate, minor), **documentation**, **onset** and **patient factors**. The pharmacist screens every prescription, explains the mechanism, and suggests a safe alternative, dose change, timing change or monitoring.

## Requirements

Case sheets, interaction reference (book or database), National Formulary of India or similar reference, interaction reporting form, calculator.

## Procedure

1. List all drugs (prescription, OTC, herbal) with dose and start date.
2. Check every pair against an interaction reference.
3. For each interaction note: drugs involved, mechanism, expected effect, severity, onset and documentation.
4. Decide whether the interaction is clinically important in **this** patient.
5. Recommend management – avoid, substitute, change dose, separate doses, monitor.
6. Communicate to the prescriber and document; counsel the patient.

## Observations

**Case 1.** A 62-year-old man taking **simvastatin 40 mg** at night for high cholesterol is prescribed **clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily** for 7 days for a chest infection. After 4 days he complains of muscle pain and weakness; urine is dark.

| Item | Record |
| --- | --- |
| Object / precipitant | Simvastatin / clarithromycin |
| Type and mechanism | Pharmacokinetic – clarithromycin strongly inhibits the CYP3A4 enzyme that metabolises simvastatin → simvastatin levels rise |
| Effect | Myopathy, possibly rhabdomyolysis (dark urine, kidney damage) |
| Severity | Major – combination generally avoided |
| Recommendation | Stop simvastatin during the antibiotic course (or choose an antibiotic without this effect, such as amoxicillin if suitable); check CK and kidney function urgently; restart statin after the course if CK normal |
| Counselling | Report muscle pain or dark urine at once while on statins; tell every doctor about the statin |

**Case 2.** A 25-year-old woman on a **combined oral contraceptive pill** is started on anti-TB treatment containing **rifampicin**.

| Item | Record |
| --- | --- |
| Object / precipitant | Oral contraceptive (ethinylestradiol + progestin) / rifampicin |
| Type and mechanism | Pharmacokinetic – rifampicin is a strong **enzyme inducer**, increasing metabolism of the hormones → lower levels |
| Effect | Contraceptive failure (unplanned pregnancy), breakthrough bleeding |
| Onset | Delayed – induction builds up over 1–2 weeks and persists for some weeks after stopping rifampicin |
| Severity | Major |
| Recommendation | Use a reliable non-hormonal method (for example a copper IUCD or barrier method) during rifampicin therapy and for the period advised after stopping it |
| Counselling | Explain why the pill may fail; use the advised method consistently |

### Worked format for reporting (example)

```text
Patient: Mr A, 62 y        Ward: Medicine         Date: __/__/__
Drugs: simvastatin 40 mg HS; clarithromycin 500 mg BD
Interaction: clarithromycin (CYP3A4 inhibitor) ↑ simvastatin → myopathy
Severity: major; Onset: within days; Documentation: established
Recommendation: withhold simvastatin during course; check CK, creatinine
Accepted by prescriber: Yes / No     Outcome: _______________
Pharmacist: ________________
```

## Result

Two clinically significant drug–drug interactions were identified, their mechanisms explained and management recommended and documented.

## Precautions

1. Include OTC and herbal products in the drug list.
2. Not every listed interaction matters for every patient – judge clinical significance.
3. Give practical alternatives, not only warnings.
4. Remember delayed onset and offset of enzyme induction.
5. Document the prescriber's decision and the outcome.

## Viva questions

1. **Name two enzyme inducers.** Rifampicin, carbamazepine (also phenytoin, phenobarbital).
2. **Name two enzyme inhibitors.** Clarithromycin, ketoconazole (also erythromycin, fluconazole, cimetidine, grapefruit juice).
3. **Give a pharmacodynamic interaction.** Sildenafil + nitrates → severe hypotension.
4. **Give a useful interaction.** Probenecid raises penicillin levels; levodopa with carbidopa.
5. **Why are narrow therapeutic index drugs important in interactions?** Small changes in level can cause toxicity or failure (warfarin, digoxin, lithium, phenytoin).

# Wound dressing (simulated cases and role play)

**Aim:** To demonstrate the aseptic dressing of a wound in two simulated cases and to select a suitable dressing material.

## Principle

A **wound** is a break in the continuity of skin or tissue. Dressing a wound keeps it clean, absorbs discharge, keeps a moist healing surface where suitable, prevents infection and protects it from injury. Dressing is done by an **aseptic (no-touch) technique** so that no new organisms enter the wound. The choice of dressing depends on the type of wound and the amount of exudate.

## Requirements

Sterile dressing pack (gauze, cotton balls, forceps, gallipot, drape), sterile gloves, normal saline, antiseptic as per hospital policy (for example povidone-iodine), dressing materials (sterile gauze pads, paraffin gauze, transparent film, foam or hydrocolloid as available), adhesive tape or bandage, scissors, waste bags (yellow for soiled dressings), sharps container, mannequin or role-play volunteer, documentation sheet.

## Common dressing materials

| Dressing | Suitable for |
| --- | --- |
| Dry sterile gauze | Clean surgical wounds with little exudate; cover dressing |
| Paraffin gauze (tulle) | Superficial burns and abrasions – does not stick |
| Transparent film | Clean shallow wounds, IV cannula sites; allows viewing |
| Hydrocolloid | Light to moderate exudate, pressure ulcers |
| Hydrogel | Dry wounds, to add moisture |
| Foam | Moderate to heavy exudate |
| Alginate | Heavy exudate, slight bleeding |

## Procedure

1. Check the order and the patient's identity; explain the procedure and get consent; ensure privacy; give pain relief beforehand if needed.
2. Wash hands; put on clean gloves; position the patient comfortably and expose only the wound area.
3. Remove the old dressing gently (moisten with saline if stuck); look at it for amount and type of discharge; discard in the yellow bag; remove gloves and wash hands.
4. Open the sterile pack on a clean trolley without touching the inside; pour saline into the gallipot; put on sterile gloves.
5. **Assess the wound:** site, size, depth, colour of the wound bed, exudate, smell, edges, signs of infection (redness, swelling, heat, pus, fever).
6. **Clean the wound** with saline-soaked swabs using forceps, from the cleanest area to the dirtiest – for a clean incision, from the wound outward, one stroke per swab; discard each swab after one stroke.
7. Apply antiseptic only if prescribed by the hospital policy; dry the surrounding skin.
8. Apply the chosen dressing so that it covers the wound with a margin; secure with tape or bandage (not too tight).
9. Dispose of waste: soiled dressings in yellow bags, sharps in the sharps container; remove gloves; wash hands.
10. **Document:** date, wound appearance and size, dressing used, patient's response, next dressing date.

## Observations (simulated cases)

| Case | Wound description | Dressing chosen | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Post-operative abdominal incision, day 3 | Clean, dry, edges joined, no redness | Dry sterile gauze pad / film | Clean wound with minimal exudate |
| 2. Superficial burn on forearm (scald) | Red, moist, small blisters | Paraffin gauze covered with sterile gauze and light bandage | Non-adherent; protects and allows healing |

Role play: one student acts as the pharmacist/dresser, one as the patient; the observer checks steps against a checklist (hand hygiene, aseptic technique, cleaning direction, waste disposal, documentation).

## Result

Aseptic wound dressing was demonstrated for two simulated cases with appropriate dressing selection, waste disposal and documentation.

## Precautions

1. Hand hygiene before and after every step; maintain asepsis.
2. One swab, one stroke; never go back from a dirty area to a clean one.
3. Do not use cotton wool directly on an open wound.
4. Report signs of infection to the doctor; a swab for culture may be needed.
5. Do not apply bandages too tightly.

## Viva questions

1. **What are the signs of wound infection?** Redness, swelling, heat, pain, pus, foul smell, fever.
2. **Which solution is commonly used for cleaning wounds?** Sterile normal saline.
3. **Which dressing is non-adherent for burns?** Paraffin gauze (tulle).
4. **In which bag are soiled dressings discarded?** Yellow bag.
5. **Why clean from clean to dirty?** To avoid carrying organisms into the cleaner area.

# Vaccination and injection techniques (IV, IM, SC) using mannequins

**Aim:** To demonstrate on mannequins the techniques of intramuscular, subcutaneous, intradermal and intravenous injection and of vaccination (five activities).

> Follow the current national immunisation schedule and your institution's protocol; the details below are for practice on mannequins.

## Principle

The **route** decides the speed and site of drug action. Each route has a correct **site, needle size and angle**. Safe injection practice protects the patient (right drug, dose, site, asepsis), the health worker (no needle-stick injury) and the community (safe disposal).

| Route | Usual angle | Common sites | Typical needle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Intradermal (ID) | 10–15°, bevel up | Inner forearm; upper arm for BCG | 26–27 G, short |
| Subcutaneous (SC) | 45° (90° with short needle and skin pinched) | Abdomen, outer upper arm, front of thigh | 25–27 G |
| Intramuscular (IM) | 90° | Deltoid (small volumes), vastus lateralis (thigh – infants), ventrogluteal, dorsogluteal | 21–23 G, about 2.5 cm (shorter for infants) |
| Intravenous (IV) | 15–30° | Veins of the forearm, back of hand, antecubital fossa | Needle or cannula 18–24 G |

## Requirements

Injection-training mannequins (arm, thigh, buttock), syringes and needles of different sizes, IV cannula and set, ampoules and vials of water for injection (practice), alcohol swabs, cotton, tourniquet, gloves, kidney tray, sharps container, vaccine carrier with ice packs (demonstration), immunisation card.

## Procedure

### Common steps (all routes)

1. Check the prescription/immunisation schedule: right patient, drug, dose, route, time; check expiry and appearance; check allergy.
2. Wash hands; wear gloves; prepare the drug aseptically (swab vial top, draw up, expel air).
3. Explain the procedure; position the patient; select and expose the site.
4. Clean the site as per protocol and allow it to dry.
5. Inject at the correct angle and depth; inject slowly; withdraw the needle quickly; press gently with dry cotton (do not massage for insulin or vaccines unless advised).
6. **Do not recap**; discard the needle and syringe immediately in the sharps container.
7. Observe the patient (for vaccines, about 30 minutes for reactions); document.

### Activity 1 – Intramuscular injection

1. Deltoid: locate the dense part of the muscle about 2–3 finger-breadths below the acromion; use for small volumes.
2. Vastus lateralis: middle third of the outer thigh – preferred site in infants.
3. Stretch the skin, insert the needle at 90° with a quick dart, inject slowly.
4. **Z-track technique** (for irritant drugs such as iron): pull the skin to one side before injecting, release after withdrawing so the track is sealed.

### Activity 2 – Subcutaneous injection

1. Pinch a fold of skin of the abdomen (away from the navel), upper arm or thigh.
2. Insert at 45° (or 90° with short insulin needles); inject; release the fold; withdraw.
3. Rotate sites (for example insulin) to avoid lumps of fat.

### Activity 3 – Intradermal injection

1. Stretch the skin of the inner forearm (or upper arm for BCG).
2. Insert the needle bevel up at 10–15°, just under the skin surface.
3. Inject slowly – a small pale bleb (wheal) should appear; do not massage.

### Activity 4 – Intravenous injection / cannulation

1. Apply a tourniquet above the site; ask the patient to open and close the fist; select a straight, visible vein.
2. Clean the site; anchor the vein by stretching the skin below it.
3. Insert the needle or cannula bevel up at 15–30°; look for "flashback" of blood.
4. Release the tourniquet; inject slowly or connect the IV set; secure the cannula with a sterile dressing and label with the date.

### Activity 5 – Vaccination (immunisation session)

1. Keep vaccines in a vaccine carrier with conditioned ice packs; check the label, expiry and VVM; do not use frozen freeze-sensitive vaccine.
2. Check the child's immunisation card and age; screen for contraindications.
3. Give each vaccine by its correct route and site as per the national schedule – for example **BCG intradermally** in the left upper arm, **oral polio vaccine** as drops by mouth, **hepatitis B and pentavalent vaccines intramuscularly** in the anterolateral thigh of infants, **measles–rubella vaccine subcutaneously** in the right upper arm.
4. Record on the card and register; tell the parent about common reactions (fever, pain) and the next due date; observe for 30 minutes.

## Observations

| Activity | Route | Site | Angle | Needle used | Done correctly |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | IM | Deltoid / vastus lateralis | 90° | 23 G | ✓ |
| 2 | SC | Abdomen | 45° | 26 G | ✓ |
| 3 | ID | Forearm | 10–15° | 26 G | ✓ |
| 4 | IV | Forearm vein | 15–30° | 20 G cannula | ✓ |
| 5 | Vaccination | As per vaccine | As per route | AD syringe | ✓ |

## Result

Intramuscular, subcutaneous, intradermal and intravenous injection techniques and vaccination were demonstrated correctly on mannequins.

## Precautions

1. Strict asepsis; one needle and syringe per injection.
2. Never recap used needles; dispose at once in sharps containers.
3. Avoid the sciatic nerve region (use the correct gluteal landmarks or other sites).
4. Check for air in syringes and IV lines.
5. Keep adrenaline and an anaphylaxis kit ready during vaccination and injections.

## Viva questions

1. **What angle is used for an IM injection?** 90°.
2. **Which IM site is preferred in infants?** Vastus lateralis (anterolateral thigh).
3. **What sign shows a correct intradermal injection?** A small pale bleb (wheal) at the site.
4. **What is the Z-track technique?** Displacing the skin before IM injection so the needle track is sealed – used for irritant drugs such as iron.
5. **Which syringe is used in immunisation?** Auto-disable syringe.

# Use of hospital pharmacy software and digital health tools

**Aim:** To use hospital pharmacy software (or a training/demo version) for prescription processing, stock management and reports, and to become familiar with common digital health tools.

## Principle

Hospital pharmacy software links prescriptions, patient profiles, stock and billing. It checks doses and interactions, keeps legal registers, raises reorder and expiry alerts and prepares reports. Digital health tools such as electronic health records, online ADR reporting, drug databases and telemedicine platforms support safe medicine use.

## Requirements

Computers with a hospital information system (HIS) pharmacy module, the hospital's own software, or a demonstration/training version; internet access; sample prescriptions and stock data; printer.

## Procedure

1. **Log in** with your own user name and password (never share passwords).
2. **Patient registration / search:** find the patient by hospital number or name; check allergies and weight in the profile.
3. **Prescription entry or receipt (CPOE):** open the electronic order; check drug, dose, frequency, route and duration; note any **interaction or dose alert** and how it is handled.
4. **Dispensing:** select batch by FEFO; print labels; record quantity issued; generate the bill or free-supply entry.
5. **Ward indent:** receive an electronic indent from a ward; approve quantities; issue and update stock.
6. **Stock management:** view current stock of an item; generate the **reorder report** (items at or below reorder level), **near-expiry report** and **ABC analysis** of consumption.
7. **Purchase:** create a purchase order; enter a goods received note (GRN) with batch, expiry and quantity.
8. **Controlled drugs:** view the electronic narcotic or Schedule H1 register and running balance.
9. **Digital health tools (demonstration):**
   - online/app-based ADR reporting under PvPI;
   - drug information and interaction databases;
   - electronic health record view (discharge summary, lab results);
   - the ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account) concept for linking records;
   - teleconsultation platforms such as the government's eSanjeevani service.
10. Log out; never leave a logged-in screen unattended.

## Observations (sample exercise)

| Task | Output / remark |
| --- | --- |
| Prescription checked | Ceftriaxone 1 g IV BD, patient CrCl normal – no alert |
| Interaction alert seen | Clarithromycin + simvastatin – major; pharmacist informed prescriber |
| Batch selected | Batch with earliest expiry (FEFO) |
| Reorder report | 6 items at or below reorder level → purchase indent raised |
| Near-expiry report | 3 items expiring within 3 months → transfer/return planned |
| ABC report | A-class items: ___ % of items, ___ % of value |
| GRN entry | Batch, expiry, quantity, rate entered and verified |

**Check of a software reorder calculation:** average daily use 40 units, lead time 7 days, safety stock 120 units.

```text
Reorder level = (40 × 7) + 120 = 400 units
The software should flag the item when stock falls to 400 units.
```

## Result

Hospital pharmacy software was used for prescription processing, dispensing, indents, stock and expiry reports, purchase entries and controlled drug registers, and common digital health tools were demonstrated.

## Precautions

1. Keep passwords secret; log out after use.
2. Respect patient confidentiality; do not copy or share patient data.
3. Do not ignore alerts without checking; document the reason for any override.
4. Verify that stock in the software matches physical stock (periodic verification).
5. Keep back-up and a manual procedure for system failure.

## Viva questions

1. **What is CPOE?** Computerised prescriber order entry – doctors enter orders electronically.
2. **Name two reports a pharmacy system generates.** Reorder report, near-expiry report (also ABC, consumption, narcotic register).
3. **What is an EHR?** An electronic health record – a shareable digital record of a person's health information.
4. **What is alert fatigue?** Ignoring warnings because the system shows too many of them.
5. **Why is an audit trail important?** It records who did what and when, which is essential for controlled drugs and accountability.
practicals.title: Use of hospital pharmacy software and digital health tools

1. Definition: hospital pharmacy is the department or service of a hospital, run by registered pharmacists, responsible for selection, procurement, storage, preparation, distribution and safe use of medicines and medical supplies for in-patients and out-patients, and for drug information.
2. Scope: (a) procurement and inventory control; (b) dispensing to OPD and distribution to wards, ICU, OT; (c) bulk compounding, sterile products, IV admixtures, TPN; (d) clinical services – ward rounds, chart review, ADR monitoring, counselling; (e) drug information; (f) committee work – P&T, infection control, antimicrobial stewardship; (g) special services – radiopharmacy, poison information; (h) education and research; (i) quality and safety for NABH/NQAS.

questions.answer:

Responsibilities: follow the formulary and drug policies; purchase and store quality medicines; dispense correctly with labels and counselling; run an efficient ward distribution system; control NDPS and Schedule H1 drugs; prepare sterile and non-sterile products, IV admixtures and TPN; provide drug information; monitor ADRs and prevent errors; serve on P&T and infection control committees; train staff; keep legal records.
2. Qualification: D.Pharm or B.Pharm with registration in the State Pharmacy Council (compulsory under the Pharmacy Act, 1948); senior posts need higher degrees and experience as per recruitment rules; clinical pharmacists – Pharm.D or M.Pharm (Pharmacy Practice).

questions.answer:
1. NABH = National Accreditation Board for Hospitals and Healthcare Providers, a constituent board of the Quality Council of India; it accredits hospitals that meet its quality standards (voluntary).
2. Standards are arranged in chapters; Management of Medication (MOM) is the pharmacy chapter; Hospital Infection Control and Patient Safety and Quality Improvement are related.
3. Pharmacist's role: (a) prepare and update the formulary with the committee; (b) safe storage – temperature logs, security, separation of LASA and high-risk drugs; (c) check emergency trolleys; (d) ensure prescriptions are legible, dated, signed, without unsafe abbreviations; (e) dispense after pharmacist check with labels and FEFO; (f) identify and handle high-alert drugs; (g) ADR and medication error reporting, analysis and presentation at quality meetings; (h) policies on narcotics, recall, expired drugs, patients' own medicines; (i) write SOPs and train staff; (j) take part in audits and indicators.
4. NQAS = National Quality Assurance Standards for public health facilities, developed by NHSRC under MoHFW; facilities assessed in eight areas of concern: service provision, patient rights, inputs, support services, clinical services, infection control, quality management and outcome.
5. Pharmacist in NQAS: no stock-outs of essential drugs, cold chain, FEFO, records, counselling, help in audits.

1. Definition: an advisory and policy-making body of physicians, pharmacists, nurses and administrators that acts as the link between the medical staff and the pharmacy and decides all matters on selection and use of drugs in the hospital.
2. Objectives: (a) advisory – advise staff and administration on drugs; (b) educational – keep staff up to date; (c) drug policy – develop formulary and drug-use policies; (d) promote rational, safe and economical drug use.
3. Composition: chairperson – senior physician or medical superintendent; members – heads of major clinical departments; secretary – chief pharmacist; nursing superintendent; administrator/finance officer; microbiologist and clinical pharmacologist/clinical pharmacist as needed; meets regularly (every 2–3 months), minutes kept.
4. Functions: prepare and revise hospital formulary; evaluate new drug requests; frame policies – generic substitution, non-formulary drugs, medical representatives and samples, investigational drugs, automatic stop orders, patients' own drugs; monitor ADRs and medication errors; drug use evaluation; antibiotic policy and standard treatment guidelines; approve emergency drug lists; education through bulletins; advise on purchase and quality.
questions.question: Define Pharmacy and Therapeutics Committee. Write its objectives, composition and functions.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a continually revised list of drugs approved for use in the hospital by the P&T Committee, with important information on each, reflecting current clinical judgement of the medical staff.
2. Contents: title and introduction with committee members; hospital policies and procedures (formulary policy, non-formulary request, prescription rules, stop orders, narcotic rules, ADR reporting); drug listing by therapeutic category – generic name, brands, dosage forms and strengths stocked, dose, indications, contraindications, ADRs, interactions, special notes; special information – interaction tables, IV compatibility, renal doses, antidotes, lab values, abbreviations; indexes.
3. Development: committee decides → pharmacist lists drugs in use with consumption and cost → grouped by therapeutic class → departments review → selection on efficacy, safety, need, total cost, NLEM, no duplication → pharmacist writes monographs → draft circulated → approval → printing/electronic distribution → regular (yearly) revision.
4. Use: prescribing from it; non-formulary drugs only on justified request; purchase limited to formulary items; reference for nurses and pharmacists; generic substitution; training.
5. Advantages: rational and cheaper therapy, smaller inventory, better purchase terms; limitation: needs regular updating.

questions.answer:
1. Infection Control Committee: multidisciplinary committee that plans, carries out and monitors the programme to prevent hospital-acquired infections (infections appearing usually 48 h or more after admission).
2. Composition: medical superintendent or senior clinician (chair), microbiologist (often secretary), infection control nurses, heads of medicine, surgery, paediatrics, ICU, OT, chief pharmacist, nursing superintendent, CSSD, housekeeping, engineering.
3. Functions: policies on hand hygiene, isolation, sterilisation and disinfection, bio-medical waste; surveillance and outbreak investigation; antibiotic policy and antibiogram; choice and dilution of disinfectants; staff training and vaccination; needle-stick policy.
4. AMR: survival of microbes despite antimicrobials; caused by unnecessary or wrong antibiotic use, OTC sale, poor infection control, poor adherence.
5. Pharmacist's role: prepare antibiotic policy; restricted (reserve) antibiotics only with approval; review every antibiotic order (indication, dose, duration, renal adjustment); antimicrobial stewardship – de-escalation, IV-to-oral switch, stop unnecessary combinations; automatic stop orders; monitor consumption (DDD per 100 bed-days); no sale without prescription, Schedule H1 register; counsel patients to complete course; educate staff; AWaRe classification (Access, Watch, Reserve).

questions.answer: WHO groups antibiotics to guide stewardship: (1) Access – first-choice drugs with lower resistance potential, e.g., amoxicillin; (2) Watch – higher resistance potential, use for specific indications, e.g., ceftriaxone, azithromycin, meropenem; (3) Reserve – last-resort drugs for multi-drug-resistant infections, e.g., colistin, linezolid, tigecycline. Hospitals use it to restrict Reserve drugs and monitor Watch drugs.

1. Tender: formal written invitation to suppliers to quote prices for specified items under stated conditions; the contract goes to the lowest acceptable qualified bidder (L1).
2. Types: open (advertised) tender; limited tender (registered suppliers only); single tender (only one source).
3. Steps: prepare list with specifications (generic name, strength, IP/BP standard, pack, shelf life on delivery) and quantity → tender notice with last date → bidders submit EMD, technical bid and price bid separately (two-bid system) → technical bids opened (licences, GMP certificate, turnover, non-conviction, quality reports) → price bids of qualified firms opened → comparative statement → purchase committee approves L1 → rate/supply contract and performance security; EMD of others returned → purchase orders, receipt, quality check, payment.
4. E-tender: same process online through CPPP, state portals or GeM; transparent, wider participation, less paperwork, faster; needs internet, digital signatures, trained staff.
5. Quotation method: for small or urgent buys; quotations from at least three suppliers, comparative statement, order to lowest acceptable rate; quicker but less competitive.

questions.answer:
1. EOQ = the order size at which the total of annual ordering cost and carrying cost is minimum; EOQ = √(2DS/H), D = annual demand, S = cost per order, H = carrying cost per unit per year.
2. Example: D = 3,600 vials, S = Rs 200, H = Rs 4 → EOQ = √(2 × 3600 × 200 / 4) = √360,000 = 600 vials; 6 orders a year; ordering cost 6 × 200 = Rs 1,200; average stock 300 × 4 = Rs 1,200 carrying cost; total Rs 2,400 (minimum; equal ordering and carrying costs).
3. Lead time = time from order to receipt. Safety stock = (maximum daily use − normal daily use) × lead time.
4. Reorder level = normal daily use × lead time + safety stock. Example: normal use 50/day, maximum 70/day, lead time 10 days → safety stock (70 − 50) × 10 = 200; ROL = 500 + 200 = 700 units.
5. Maximum stock = ROL + ROQ − (minimum use × minimum lead time); limitations of EOQ – assumes steady demand and price.

questions.answer:
1. ABC analysis: items classified by annual consumption value (quantity × unit cost) – A ≈ 10–20% of items, ≈ 70% of value (strict control); B ≈ 20–30% items, ≈ 20% value (moderate); C ≈ 60–70% items, ≈ 10% value (simple control).
2. Steps: list items → annual value → arrange descending → cumulative % of value and items → cut-off.
3. Example: of 14 items worth Rs 30 lakh, meropenem, albumin and insulin (3 items, 21%) used 66.7% of money – class A; next 4 items 22.7% – B; remaining 7 items 10.7% – C.
4. VED: by criticality – Vital (life-saving, never out of stock: adrenaline, insulin, ASV), Essential (short stock-out tolerable: most antibiotics), Desirable (little harm if absent: vitamins, tonics).
5. ABC–VED matrix: category I – AV, AE, AD, BV, CV (top management attention); category II – BE, CE, BD; category III – CD (least control). E.g., meropenem in ICU = AV (I); vitamin B-complex = CD (III).
6. Other analyses: FSN (fast, slow, non-moving), SDE (scarce, difficult, easy), HML (high, medium, low unit cost).
questions.question: Explain ABC and VED analysis with an example. What is the ABC–VED matrix?

questions.answer: Average inventory = (8 + 12)/2 = Rs 10 lakh. Inventory turnover = consumption ÷ average inventory = 60 ÷ 10 = 6 times a year. Days of stock = 365 ÷ 6 ≈ 61 days. Interpretation: on average about two months' stock is held; a higher turnover means less money blocked, a very low turnover means overstocking and expiry risk.

Precautions: separate storage with red 'High Alert' labels; concentrated KCl not kept on wards; independent double check before administration; standard concentrations; limited access; staff training.

questions.answer:
1. Central drug store: main storage point for receipt, checking, storage and issue of medicines and supplies; ground floor near loading bay; one-way flow receive → check → quarantine → store → issue.
2. Storage conditions: as per label/IP – freezer about −25 to −10 °C, refrigerator 2–8 °C, cool place 8–25 °C, protect from light and moisture; temperature and humidity logged twice daily; racks off the floor and away from walls; heavy items low.
3. Separate areas: NDPS (double lock), Schedule H1 and high-alert, inflammables, corrosives, external preparations, LASA kept apart, expired/rejected/recalled segregated; pest control; restricted access.
4. Methods of storage: alphabetical by generic name; pharmacological/therapeutic class; dosage form; frequency of use; manufacturer; bin-coded locations – usually a combination (dosage form, then alphabetical) with bin cards.
5. Distribution: indents from wards/sub-stores on fixed days → pharmacist checks quantities → items picked by FEFO → issue voucher signed → records updated; special indents for NDPS and H1 drugs.
questions.question: Describe the inventory management of the central drug store with respect to storage conditions, methods of storage and distribution.

questions.answer:
1. Cold chain: system of people, equipment and procedures keeping temperature-sensitive products (vaccines, insulin, biologicals, oxytocin) within the recommended range, usually +2 to +8 °C, from manufacturer to patient.
2. Importance: heat damage is cumulative and irreversible; freezing destroys freeze-sensitive vaccines (HepB, pentavalent, DPT, Td, IPV, PCV); damaged vaccine looks normal.
3. Devices: pharmacy refrigerator (2–8 °C); ice-lined refrigerator (top-opening, ice lining holds 2–8 °C during long power cuts; freeze-sensitive vaccines kept in the upper basket); deep freezer (about −15 to −25 °C for ice packs and freezable vaccines); walk-in cooler (2–8 °C bulk) and walk-in freezer (about −15 to −25 °C) at state/regional stores; cold boxes and vaccine carriers with conditioned ice packs for transport.
4. Precautions: thermometer or data logger in each unit, temperature recorded twice daily; minimal door opening; no food; unit away from wall and sunlight; conditioned ice packs; check VVM (inner square lighter than circle = usable); shake test if freezing suspected; contingency plan for power failure; FEFO.
questions.question: What is cold chain? Describe the devices used for cold storage and the precautions in maintaining the cold chain.

questions.answer:
1. Monthly expiry check; near-expiry list (e.g., next 3 months) circulated for use or transfer; return to supplier where contract permits replacement.
2. Expired items removed immediately, marked 'Expired – not for use', kept in separate locked area, entered in expired drugs register (name, batch, quantity, value, expiry).
3. Condemnation committee approves write-off; disposal as per Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 – discarded/expired medicines are yellow category; returned to manufacturer or sent to common bio-medical waste treatment facility for incineration; aerosols not burned; no antibiotics or cytotoxics into drains.
4. Narcotics: remain locked and recorded until destroyed by a committee in the manner allowed under the NDPS Act and state rules; destruction certificate signed; NDPS register closed; partly used ampoules discarded with a witness, both sign; empty ampoules returned.
5. Cytotoxic drugs: yellow bags/containers labelled 'Cytotoxic'; returned to manufacturer or incinerated above 1200 °C; handlers wear gloves, gown, mask, eye protection; spill kit available.

questions.answer:
FIFO (first in, first out): stock received first is issued first – based on date of receipt.
FEFO (first expiry, first out): stock with the earliest expiry is issued first, whatever the date of receipt – preferred for medicines.
Example: batch A received in January expires next year; batch B received in March expires next June – FIFO issues A first, FEFO issues B first, avoiding expiry. New stock is placed behind old stock with expiry written boldly.

Purchase: requirement/indent, tender papers and comparative statement, supply/rate contract, purchase order, delivery challan and invoice, goods received note, quality test reports, payment records.
Inventory: stock register/ledger (with batch and expiry), bin cards, indent book and issue vouchers, NDPS register, Schedule H1 register, expiry register, cold chain temperature log, physical stock verification report, condemnation register.

questions.answer: ILR is a top-opening refrigerator with a lining of water-filled tubes or ice packs around the cabinet; the ice keeps the inside at +2 to +8 °C during long power cuts. Used at hospitals and PHCs for vaccines. Vaccines are kept in the baskets provided; freeze-sensitive vaccines (HepB, pentavalent, DPT, Td, IPV) in the upper part away from the cold walls; temperature recorded twice daily with a thermometer; door opened as little as possible.

questions.answer: A heat-sensitive label on a vaccine vial that darkens with cumulative heat exposure. Reading: if the inner square is lighter than the outer circle, the vaccine can be used (if not expired); if the square matches or is darker than the circle, the vaccine has had too much heat and must be discarded. VVM does not show freezing damage – for that the shake test is used.

questions.answer:
1. Unit dose = single dose packed and labelled ready to administer. Unit dose drug distribution = pharmacist-coordinated system in which medicines are dispensed in unit-dose packages ready to administer and not more than 24 hours' supply is on the ward at any time.
2. Procedure: doctor's order (copy or electronic) to pharmacy → pharmacist enters into patient medication profile, checks dose, allergy, interactions → patient-specific drawer of a medication cart filled for 24 h, second check → cart exchanged on ward daily; returned doses credited → nurse gives each dose and records on MAR → new orders supplied in between.
3. Types: centralised (main pharmacy) or decentralised (satellite pharmacies).
4. Example: bed 12 on amoxicillin TDS, pantoprazole OD, paracetamol QID, enoxaparin OD → 9 labelled doses in the 24 h drawer.
5. Advantages: fewest medication errors; less wastage and pilferage; credit for unused doses; small ward stock; accurate charges; more nursing time; pharmacist involved in therapy.
6. Disadvantages: high initial cost (packaging machines, carts, software); more pharmacy staff and longer hours; not all drugs available as unit doses (repackaging); needs good communication.
questions.question: Define unit dose drug distribution system. Describe its procedure, advantages and disadvantages.

questions.answer:
1. Individual prescription order: doctor's order for each patient sent to pharmacy; pharmacist dispenses patient's medicines in labelled containers, usually for several days.
Advantages: every order reviewed by pharmacist; close team contact; correct billing; better inventory control than floor stock.
Disadvantages: delay in supply; more pharmacy staff; several days' stock on ward → wastage, returns; nurses still prepare doses.
2. Floor stock: stock of common drugs kept on wards; nurses take doses as ordered; charged or non-charged (free) floor stock.
Advantages: immediate availability; fewer orders to pharmacy; fewer pharmacy staff; fewer returns.
Disadvantages: no pharmacist review → more medication errors; large ward stock → money blocked, expiry, pilferage; more nurse workload; poor storage on wards; difficult charging.
3. Floor stock suits emergency, OT and cheap common items; par level = average daily use × restock interval + buffer.
4. Most hospitals use a combination; unit dose and drug basket systems overcome many disadvantages.
questions.question: Compare individual prescription order system and floor stock system of drug distribution with their advantages and disadvantages.

questions.answer:
1. Law: NDPS Act, 1985 and rules; strict records.
2. Storage: steel cupboard with two separate locks fixed to wall; keys with pharmacist in charge and sister-in-charge; keys and stock handed over with count at shift change; separate shelf for each drug; nothing else in the cupboard.
3. Distribution: only on written order/special indent signed by a registered medical practitioner; small fixed ward stock replaced only when empty ampoules and administration record are returned; narcotic register on ward and in pharmacy – date, patient, bed, drug, dose, quantity, balance, signatures of giver and witness; unused part discarded with witness; count every shift; discrepancy reported; expired stock kept until destroyed by committee.
4. ICU/ICCU/NICU/emergency: sealed crash cart checked daily and after use; par-level floor stock or automated dispensing cabinet; satellite 24-hour pharmacy; standard infusion concentrations; NICU – weight-based small doses, oral syringes, preservative-free products; emergency – rapid antidotes and ASV; refrigerated items with temperature log; narcotics under double lock.

questions.answer:
1. Pharmacy prepares a separate labelled basket or tray for each patient (name, bed number) containing that patient's medicines for a fixed period, usually 24 hours, from current orders.
2. Baskets go to the ward in a trolley; nurse gives doses from the patient's basket; basket returns for daily refill.
3. Advantages: patient's medicines kept separate, daily pharmacist check, small ward stock, easy credit of returns, cheaper than full unit dose.
4. Disadvantages: doses may not be individually labelled unit doses; daily filling and transport; extra supply needed when orders change.

questions.answer:
Machines and software that store, count, pack, dispense and track medicines: automated dispensing cabinets on wards (open only the right drawer for a verified order), central pharmacy robots, tablet counting machines, unit-dose packaging machines, carousels, barcode medication administration, smart infusion pumps, CPOE.
Advantages: fewer errors, better stock control and security of controlled drugs, instant records, staff time saved.
Disadvantages: high cost, power/software failure, training needed, alert overrides; pharmacist check still essential.

Disadvantages: no pharmacist review of each order → more medication errors; large ward stock blocks money and leads to expiry and pilferage; more nurse workload; poor storage on wards; difficult to charge patients correctly. Charged and non-charged (free) floor stock are its two types.

questions.answer:
1. IV admixture: sterile solution made by adding one or more drugs to a large-volume parenteral fluid (5% dextrose, normal saline) for IV infusion. IV admixture service: centralised pharmacy service where trained staff prepare these under aseptic conditions.
2. Facilities: clean room with HEPA-filtered air; horizontal laminar air flow workbench for routine admixtures; vertical LAF/Class II biological safety cabinet for cytotoxics (protects operator).
3. Procedure: check order and compatibility → gowning, hand washing, alcohol-wiped surfaces → aseptic technique (work well inside hood, swab ports, sterile syringes, filter needles for ampoules) → inspect against light/dark background → label (patient, drug, dose, fluid, volume, rate, time prepared, expiry, initials) → store and deliver.
4. Incompatibilities: physical – precipitation (Ca + PO4; Ca + bicarbonate; ceftriaxone + Ca; phenytoin in dextrose; amphotericin B in saline), colour change, gas, sorption (insulin, nitroglycerin to PVC); chemical – hydrolysis, oxidation, pH effects (ampicillin less stable in dextrose; catecholamines inactivated by bicarbonate; aminoglycoside + penicillin in same bag); therapeutic – opposing or additive effects in the body.
5. Prevention: check references, add one drug at a time, avoid additions to blood, mannitol, bicarbonate, lipids, amino acids; separate lines/flush; use promptly.
